claim: The model presents how neural representations of egocentric spatial experiences in parietal cortex interface with viewpoint-independent representations in medial temporal areas, via retrosplenial cortex.
source: We present a model of how neural representations of egocentric spatial experiences in parietal cortex interface with viewpoint-independent representations in medial temporal areas, via retrosplenial cortex, to enable many key aspects of spatial cognition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the main contribution of the model.

claim: The model predicts new cell types including egocentric and head-direction-modulated boundary- and object-vector cells.
source: This account shows how previously reported neural responses (place, head-direction and grid cells, allocentric boundary- and object-vector cells, gain-field neurons) can map onto higher cognitive function in a modular way, and predicts new cell types (egocentric and head-direction-modulated boundary- and object-vector cells).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that the model predicts these new cell types.

claim: The model predicts how neural populations interact across multiple brain regions to support spatial memory, scene construction, novelty-detection, 'trace cells', and mental navigation.
source: The model predicts how these neural populations should interact across multiple brain regions to support spatial memory, scene construction, novelty-detection, 'trace cells', and mental navigation.
evidence: The abstract explicitly lists these predicted functions.

claim: Object-vector cells allow items to be remembered within a contextual representation based on environmental boundaries.
source: Simulated behavior and firing rate maps are compared to experimental data, for example showing how object-vector cells allow items to be remembered within a contextual representation based on environmental boundaries, and how grid cells could update the viewpoint in imagery during planning and short-cutting by driving sequential place cell activity.
evidence: The abstract states this as an example of the model's capabilities.

claim: Grid cells could update the viewpoint in imagery during planning and short-cutting by driving sequential place cell activity.
source: Simulated behavior and firing rate maps are compared to experimental data, for example showing how object-vector cells allow items to be remembered within a contextual representation based on environmental boundaries, and how grid cells could update the viewpoint in imagery during planning and short-cutting by driving sequential place cell activity.
evidence: The abstract states this as an example of the model's capabilities.

claim: The ability to reconstruct perceptual experiences into imagery is one of the hallmarks of human cognition.
source: The ability to reconstruct perceptual experiences into imagery constitutes one of the hallmarks of human cognition, from the ability to imagine past episodes (Tulving 1985) to planning future scenarios (Schacter et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tulving 1985 and Schacter et al., 2007.

claim: Scene construction and episodic future thinking depend on the hippocampal system.
source: Intriguingly, this ability (also known as 'scene construction' and 'episodic future thinking') appears to depend on the hippocampal system (Schacter et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010), in which direct (spatial) correlates of the activities of single neurons have long been identified in rodents (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Taube et al., 1990a; Hafting et al., 2005) and more recently in humans (Ekstrom et al., 2003; Jacobs et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Schacter et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010.

claim: Direct spatial correlates of single neuron activities have been identified in rodents.
source: Intriguingly, this ability (also known as 'scene construction' and 'episodic future thinking') appears to depend on the hippocampal system (Schacter et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010), in which direct (spatial) correlates of the activities of single neurons have long been identified in rodents (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Taube et al., 1990a; Hafting et al., 2005) and more recently in humans (Ekstrom et al., 2003; Jacobs et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Taube et al., 1990a; Hafting et al., 2005.

claim: Direct spatial correlates of single neuron activities have been identified in humans.
source: Intriguingly, this ability (also known as 'scene construction' and 'episodic future thinking') appears to depend on the hippocampal system (Schacter et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010), in which direct (spatial) correlates of the activities of single neurons have long been identified in rodents (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Taube et al., 1990a; Hafting et al., 2005) and more recently in humans (Ekstrom et al., 2003; Jacobs et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ekstrom et al., 2003; Jacobs et al., 2010.

claim: The model extends the Byrne, Becker and Burgess model of spatial memory and imagery of empty environments.
source: Extending the Byrne, Becker and Burgess model of spatial memory and imagery of empty environments (Burgess et al., 2001a; Byrne et al., 2007), we propose a large-scale systems-level model of the interaction between Papez' circuit, parietal, retrosplenial, and medial temporal areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burgess et al., 2001a; Byrne et al., 2007.

claim: Egocentric representations of the local sensory environment are transformed into viewpoint-independent allocentric representations for long-term storage in the medial temporal lobes.
source: In brief, egocentric (i.e. body-centered) representations of the local sensory environment, corresponding to a specific point of view, are transformed into viewpoint-independent (allocentric or world-centered) representations for long-term storage in the medial temporal lobes (MTL).
evidence: This is a core claim of the model described in the introduction.

claim: The reverse process allows reconstruction of viewpoint-dependent egocentric representations from stored allocentric representations, supporting imagery and recollection.
source: The reverse process allows reconstruction of viewpoint-dependent egocentric representations from stored allocentric representations, supporting imagery and recollection.
evidence: This is a core claim of the model described in the introduction.

claim: Place cells fire when an animal traverses a specific location within the environment.
source: These include place cells (PCs), which fire when an animal traverses a specific location within the environment (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971);
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971.

claim: Head direction cells fire according to the animal's head direction relative to the external environment, irrespective of location.
source: head direction cells (HDCs), which fire according to the animal's head direction relative to the external environment, irrespective of location (Taube and Ranck, 1990; Taube et al., 1990a; Taube et al., 1990b);
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Taube and Ranck, 1990; Taube et al., 1990a; Taube et al., 1990b.

claim: Boundary vector cells fire in response to the presence of a boundary at a specific combination of distance and allocentric direction.
source: boundary vector cells (Lever et al., 2009); henceforth BVCs), which fire in response to the presence of a boundary at a specific combination of distance and allocentric direction (i.e. North, East, West, South, irrespective of an agent's orientation);
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lever et al., 2009.

claim: Grid cells exhibit multiple, regularly spaced firing fields.
source: and grid cells (GCs), which exhibit multiple, regularly spaced firing fields (Hafting et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hafting et al., 2005.

claim: Evidence for the presence of place cells, head direction cells, boundary vector cells, and grid cells in human and non-human primates is mounting steadily.
source: Evidence for the presence of these cell types in human and non-human primates is mounting steadily (Robertson et al., 1999; Ekstrom et al., 2003; Jacobs et al., 2010; Doeller et al., 2010; Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al., 2016; Nadasdy et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Robertson et al., 1999; Ekstrom et al., 2003; Jacobs et al., 2010; Doeller et al., 2010; Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al., 2016; Nadasdy et al., 2017.

claim: The egocentric representation supporting imagery has been suggested to reside in medial parietal cortex.
source: The egocentric representation supporting imagery has been suggested to reside in medial parietal cortex (e.g. the precuneus; Fletcher et al., 1996; Knauff et al., 2000; Formisano et al., 2002; Sack et al., 2002; Wallentin et al. (2006); Hebscher et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Fletcher et al., 1996; Knauff et al., 2000; Formisano et al., 2002; Sack et al., 2002; Wallentin et al. (2006); Hebscher et al., 2018.

claim: Parietal window neurons code for the presence of scene elements in peri-personal space and correspond to a representation along the dorsal visual stream.
source: Its neurons code for the presence of scene elements (boundaries, landmarks, objects) in peri-personal space (ahead, left, right) and correspond to a representation along the dorsal visual stream (the 'where' pathway; Ungerleider, 1982; Mishkin et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ungerleider, 1982; Mishkin et al., 1983.

claim: Parietal window boundary coding cells are egocentric analogues of BVCs.
source: The parietal window boundary coding (PWb) cells are egocentric analogues of BVCs (Barry et al., 2006; Lever et al., 2009), consistent with evidence that parietal areas support egocentric spatial processing (Bisiach and Luzzatti, 1978; Nitz, 2009; Save and Poucet, 2009; Wilber et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barry et al., 2006; Lever et al., 2009; Bisiach and Luzzatti, 1978; Nitz, 2009; Save and Poucet, 2009; Wilber et al., 2014.

claim: The transformation between egocentric and allocentric reference frames is performed by a gain-field circuit in retrosplenial cortex.
source: The transformation between egocentric (parietal) and allocentric (MTL) reference frames is performed by a gain-field circuit in retrosplenial cortex (Burgess et al., 2001a; Byrne et al., 2007; Wilber et al., 2014; Alexander and Nitz, 2015; Bicanski and Burgess, 2016), analogous to gain-field neurons found in posterior parietal cortex (Snyder et al., 1998; Salinas and Abbott, 1995; Pouget and Sejnowski, 1997; Pouget et al., 2002) or parieto-occipital areas (Galletti et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Burgess et al., 2001a; Byrne et al., 2007; Wilber et al., 2014; Alexander and Nitz, 2015; Bicanski and Burgess, 2016; Snyder et al., 1998; Salinas and Abbott, 1995; Pouget and Sejnowski, 1997; Pouget et al., 2002; Galletti et al., 1995.

claim: Head-direction provides the gain-modulation in the transformation circuit.
source: Head-direction provides the gain-modulation in the transformation circuit, producing directionally modulated boundary vector cells which connect egocentric and allocentric boundary coding neurons.
evidence: This is a core claim of the model architecture.

claim: The transformation between egocentric and allocentric directions requires input from head-direction cells found along Papez's circuit.
source: That this transformation between egocentric directions (left, right, ahead) and environmentally-referenced directions (nominally North, South, East, West) requires input from the head-direction cells found along Papez's circuit (Taube et al., 1990a; Taube et al., 1990b) is consistent with its involvement in episodic memory (e.g. Aggleton and Brown, 1999; Delay and Brion, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Taube et al., 1990a; Taube et al., 1990b; Aggleton and Brown, 1999; Delay and Brion, 1969.

claim: During perception the egocentric parietal window representation is based on sensory inputs and driven in a bottom-up manner.
source: During perception the egocentric parietal window representation is based on (highly processed) sensory inputs. That is, it is driven in a bottom-up manner, and the transformation circuit maps the egocentric PWb representation to allocentric BVCs.
evidence: This describes the bottom-up mode of operation in the model.

claim: When the transformation circuit acts in reverse (top-down mode), it reconstructs the parietal representation from BVCs.
source: When the transformation circuit acts in reverse (top-down mode), it reconstructs the parietal representation from BVCs which are co-active with other medial temporal cell populations, forming the substrate of viewpoint-independent (i.e. allocentric) memory.
evidence: This describes the top-down mode of operation in the model.

claim: The reverse transformation yields an orientation-specific egocentric parietal representation and constitutes the model's account of spatial imagery and explicit recall.
source: This yields an orientation-specific (egocentric) parietal representation (a specific point of view) and constitutes the model's account of (spatial) imagery and explicit recall of spatial configurations of known spaces (Burgess et al., 2001a; Byrne et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burgess et al., 2001a; Byrne et al., 2007.

claim: The model proposes allocentric object vector cells (OVCs) analogous to BVCs.
source: To account for the presence of objects within the environment, we propose allocentric object vector cells (OVCs) analogous to BVCs, and show how object-locations can be embedded into spatial memory, supported by visuo-spatial attention.
evidence: This is a novel prediction of the model.

claim: The proposed object-coding populations in the MTL map onto recently discovered neuronal populations.
source: Importantly, the proposed object-coding populations in the MTL map onto recently discovered neuronal populations (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013; Hoydal et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013; Hoydal et al., 2017.

claim: The model predicts a population of egocentric object-coding cells in the parietal window (PWo cells).
source: We also predict a population of egocentric object-coding cells in the parietal window (PWo cells: egocentric analogues to OVCs), as well as directionally modulated boundary and object coding neurons (in the transformation circuit).
evidence: This is a novel prediction of the model.

claim: The model predicts directionally modulated boundary and object coding neurons in the transformation circuit.
source: We also predict a population of egocentric object-coding cells in the parietal window (PWo cells: egocentric analogues to OVCs), as well as directionally modulated boundary and object coding neurons (in the transformation circuit).
evidence: This is a novel prediction of the model.

claim: The model includes a grid cell population to account for mental navigation and planning.
source: Finally, we include a grid cell population to account for mental navigation and planning, which drives sequential place cell firing reminiscent of hippocampal 'replay' (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011) and preplay (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011; Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2015.

claim: Cells that encode an egocentric representation of boundary locations have recently been described.
source: Intriguingly, cells that encode an egocentric representation of boundary locations (akin to parietal window neurons in the present model) have recently been described (Hinman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hinman et al., 2017.

claim: Head direction cells are arranged in a simple ring-attractor circuit.
source: Head direction cells (HDCs) are arranged in a simple ring-attractor circuit (Skaggs et al., 1995; Zhang, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Skaggs et al., 1995; Zhang, 1996.

claim: Current head direction is updated by angular velocity information as the agent explores the environment.
source: Current head direction, encoded by activity in this attractor circuit, is updated by angular velocity information as the agent explores the environment.
evidence: This describes how the head direction system operates in the model.

claim: The retrosplenial transformation circuit consists of 20 sublayers.
source: The retrosplenial transformation circuit (RSC/TR) consists of 20 sublayers.
evidence: This is a specific architectural detail of the model.

claim: Each sublayer of the transformation circuit is a copy of the BVC population, with firing tuned to a specific head-direction.
source: Each sublayer is a copy of the BVC population, with firing within each sublayer also tuned to a specific head-direction (directions are evenly spaced in the [0360] degree range).
evidence: This is a specific architectural detail of the model.

claim: Individual cells in the transformation circuit are directionally modulated boundary vector cells.
source: That is, individual cells in the transformation circuit are directionally modulated boundary vector cells, and connect egocentric (parietal) PWb neurons and allocentric BVCs (in the MTL) in a mutually consistent way.
evidence: This is a specific architectural detail of the model.

claim: All connections in the transformation circuit are reciprocal.
source: All connections are reciprocal.
evidence: This is a specific architectural detail of the model.

claim: The balance between bottom-up and top-down connections is subject to neuromodulation.
source: To implement the switch between modes of operation, we assume that the balance between bottom-up and top-down connections is subject to neuromodulation (see e.g. Hasselmo, 2006); Appendix, Equation 3 and following).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hasselmo, 2006.

claim: Connections from the parietal window to the transformation circuit are at full strength in bottom-up mode but down-regulated to 5% in top-down mode.
source: For example, connections from the parietal window (PWb and PWo) populations to the transformation circuit and thence onto BVCs/OVCs are at full strength in bottom-up mode, but down-regulated to 5% of their maximum value in top-down mode.
evidence: This is a specific implementation detail of the model.

claim: Connections from BVCs/OVCs to the transformation circuit are down-regulated during bottom-up perception and reach full strength during imagery.
source: Conversely, connections from BVCs/OVCs to the transformation circuit and onwards to the parietal window are down-regulated during bottom-up perception (5% of their maximum value) and reach full strength only during imagery (top-down reconstruction).
evidence: This is a specific implementation detail of the model.

claim: To uniquely characterize the egocentric perceptual state of encountering an object requires co-activation of perirhinal neurons and the corresponding parietal window.
source: As noted above (section "The Role of Perirhinal Neurons"), to uniquely characterize the egocentric perceptual state of encountering an object within an environment requires the co-activation of perirhinal (PRo) neurons (signaling identity) and the corresponding parietal window (PWo) (signaling location in peripersonal space).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the requirements for object representation.

claim: Maximal co-firing of only one PRo neuron with one PWo neuron at a given location is required for an unambiguous association.
source: Moreover, maximal co-firing of only one PRo neuron with one PWo neuron (or OVC, in allocentric terms) at a given location is required for an unambiguous association (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3A-C.

claim: The agent directs attention to each visible object in sequence to ensure a unique representation.
source: To ensure a unique representation, we allow the agent to direct attention to each visible object in sequence (compare Figure 3B and C; for a review of attentional mechanisms see VanRullen, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3B and C and citation to VanRullen, 2013.

claim: A fixed length for an attentional cycle is set at 600 time units.
source: We set a fixed length for an attentional cycle (600 time units).
evidence: This is a specific implementation detail of the model.

claim: Grid cell firing is thought to update the location represented by place cell firing, driven by signals relating to self-motion.
source: Grid cell (GC) firing is thought to update the location represented by place cell firing, driven by signals relating to self-motion (O'Keefe and Burgess, 2005; McNaughton et al., 2006; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Solstad et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Keefe and Burgess, 2005; McNaughton et al., 2006; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Solstad et al., 2006.

claim: During imagination, grid cell firing is driven by mock motor-efference signals and used to translate the activity bump on the sheet of place cells.
source: During imagination, we suppose that GC firing is driven by mock motor-efference signals (i.e. imagined movement without actual motor output) and used to translate the activity bump on the sheet of place cells.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about how grid cells support imagery.

claim: Both self-motion inputs via grid cells and sensory inputs converge onto place cells and may be weighted according to their reliability.
source: Importantly, both self-motion inputs (via GCs) and sensory inputs (e.g. mediated via BVCs and OVCs) converge onto PCs and both types of inputs may be weighted according to their reliability (Evans et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Evans et al., 2016.

claim: Grid cells could support place cell activity when sensory inputs are unreliable or absent.
source: GCs could thus support PC activity when sensory inputs are unreliable or absent.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the role of grid cells.

claim: Connection weights between grid cells and place cells are calculated as a simple Hebbian association.
source: Connection weights between GCs and PCs are calculated as a simple Hebbian association between PC firing at a given coordinate (according to the mapping shown in Figure 2A,B) and pre-calculated firing rate maps of GCs (7 modules with 100 cells each, see Appendix for details).
evidence: This is a specific implementation detail of the model, with reference to Figure 2A,B.

claim: Recollection in the BB-model results in visuo-spatial imagery of a coherent scene from a single viewpoint and direction.
source: Recollection in the BB-model results in visuo-spatial imagery of a coherent scene from a single viewpoint and direction, that is it implements a process of scene construction (Burgess et al., 2001a; Byrne et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010) at the neuronal level.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burgess et al., 2001a; Byrne et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010.

claim: Similar tasks in humans appear to engage the full network, including Papez' circuit, retrosplenial cortex, medial parietal areas, parahippocampus and hippocampus, and possibly the entorhinal cortex.
source: Similar tasks in humans appear to engage the full network, including Papez' circuit, where head direction cells are found (for review see Taube, 2007); retrosplenial cortex (where we hypothesize the transformation circuit to be located) (Burgess et al., 2001a; Lambrey et al., 2012; Auger and Maguire, 2013; Epstein and Vass, 2014; Marchette et al., 2014; Shine et al., 2016); medial parietal areas (Fletcher et al., 1996; Hebscher et al., 2018); parahippocampus and hippocampus (Hassabis et al., 2007; Addis et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007; Bird et al., 2010); and possibly the entorhinal cortex (Atance and O'Neill, 2001; Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al. 2016; also see Simulation 4.0).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Taube, 2007; Burgess et al., 2001a; Lambrey et al., 2012; Auger and Maguire, 2013; Epstein and Vass, 2014; Marchette et al., 2014; Shine et al., 2016; Fletcher et al., 1996; Hebscher et al., 2018; Hassabis et al., 2007; Addis et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007; Bird et al., 2010; Atance and O'Neill, 2001; Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al. 2016.

claim: BVCs were predicted by an early predecessor of the present model.
source: Notably, BVCs were predicted by an early predecessor of the present model (Hartley et al., 2000; Burgess et al., 2001a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hartley et al., 2000; Burgess et al., 2001a.

claim: OVC-like responses have been reported recently.
source: Intriguingly, OVC-like responses have been reported recently (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013; Hoydal et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013; Hoydal et al., 2017.

claim: Anatomical connections between the potential loci of BVCs/OVCs and retrosplenial cortex exist.
source: Anatomical connections between the potential loci of BVCs/OVCs and retrosplenial cortex (the suggested location of the egocentric-allocentric transformation circuit) exist. BVCs have been found in the subicular complex (Lever et al., 2009), and the related border cells and OVCs in medial entorhinal cortex (Solstad et al., 2008; Hoydal et al., 2017). Both areas receive projections from retrosplenial cortex (Jones and Witter, 2007), and project back to it (Wyss and Van Groen, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lever et al., 2009; Solstad et al., 2008; Hoydal et al., 2017; Jones and Witter, 2007; Wyss and Van Groen, 1992.

claim: Lesions along Papez' circuit have long been known to induce amnesia.
source: Lesions along Papez' circuit have long been known to induce amnesia (Delay and Brion, 1969; Squire and Slater, 1978; 1989; Parker and Gaffan, 1997; Aggleton et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Delay and Brion, 1969; Squire and Slater, 1978; 1989; Parker and Gaffan, 1997; Aggleton et al., 2016.

claim: Lesions to the fornix and mammilary bodies severely impact recollection, although recognition can be less affected.
source: Thus, lesions to the fornix and mammilary bodies severely impact recollection, although recognition can be less affected (Tsivilis et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tsivilis et al., 2008.

claim: The mammillary bodies, anterior dorsal thalamus, retrosplenial cortex, parts of the subicular complex and medial entorhinal cortex all contain head direction cells.
source: That is, the mammillary bodies (more specifically the lateral mammillary nucleus, LMN), anterior dorsal thalamus, retrosplenial cortex, parts of the subicular complex and medial entorhinal cortex all contain head direction cells (Taube, 2007; Sargolini et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Taube, 2007; Sargolini et al., 2006.

claim: In the bottom-up mode of operation, a lesion removes drive to the transformation circuit and consequently to the boundary vector cells and object vector cells.
source: In the bottom-up mode of operation (perception), the lesion removes drive to the transformation circuit and consequently to the boundary vector cells and object vector cells.
evidence: This describes the effect of a simulated lesion in the model.

claim: A lesion to Papez' circuit causes the perceived location of an object to be unable to elicit activity in the MTL and thus cannot be encoded into memory.
source: That is, the perceived location of an object (present in the egocentric parietal representation) cannot elicit activity in the MTL and thus cannot be encoded into memory (Figure 7).
evidence: This describes the effect of a simulated lesion in the model, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: The model is robust to adding firing rate noise up to 20% of peak firing rate to all cells.
source: The model is also robust to adding firing rate noise (up to 20% of peak firing rate) to all cells. Correlations between patterns at encoding and recall remain similar to the noise-free case, see Figure 8C.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Rats show a spontaneous preference for exploring novel/altered stimuli compared to familiar/unchanged ones.
source: Rats show a spontaneous preference for exploring novel/altered stimuli compared to familiar/unchanged ones.
evidence: This is a well-known behavioral phenomenon in rodents.

claim: Rats preferentially explore one of two objects that has been shifted to a new location within a given environment, a behavior impaired by hippocampal lesions.
source: We simulate one of these experiments (Mumby et al., 2002), in which rats preferentially explore one of two objects that has been shifted to a new location within a given environment, a behavior impaired by hippocampal lesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mumby et al., 2002.

claim: With an intact hippocampus, the moved object generates a significant novelty signal due to the mismatch between recalled and perceptual OVC firing.
source: With an intact hippocampus (Figure 9; Video 7), the moved object generates a significant novelty signal, due to the mismatch between recalled (top-down) OVC firing and perceptual (bottom-up) OVC firing at the encoding location.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 9 and Video 7.

claim: Detection of a change in object position requires the hippocampus.
source: That detection of a change in position requires the hippocampus is consistent with place cells binding the relative location of an object (via object vector cells) to perirhinal neurons signalling the identity of an object.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the role of the hippocampus.

claim: Rats show preferential exploration of a familiar object that was previously experienced in a different environment compared with one previously experienced in the same environment.
source: Rats also show preferential exploration of a familiar object that was previously experienced in a different environment, compared with one previously experienced in the same environment, and this preference is also abolished by hippocampal lesions (Mumby et al., 2002; Eacott and Norman, 2004; Langston and Wood, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mumby et al., 2002; Eacott and Norman, 2004; Langston and Wood, 2010.

claim: Object recognition irrespective of context is spared after hippocampal but not perirhinal lesions.
source: Finally, it has been argued that object recognition (irrespective of context) is spared after hippocampal but not perirhinal lesions (Aggleton and Brown, 1999; Winters et al., 2004; Norman and Eacott, 2004) which would be compatible with the model given that its perirhinal neuronal population signals an object's identity irrespective of location.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aggleton and Brown, 1999; Winters et al., 2004; Norman and Eacott, 2004.

claim: In rodents, it has been proposed that encoding and retrieval are gated by the theta rhythm.
source: In rodents, it has been proposed that encoding and retrieval are gated by the theta rhythm (Hasselmo et al., 2002): a constantly present modulation of the local field potential during exploration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hasselmo et al., 2002.

claim: In humans, theta is restricted to shorter bursts, but is associated with encoding and retrieval.
source: In humans, theta is restricted to shorter bursts, but is associated with encoding and retrieval (Düzel et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Düzel et al., 2010.

claim: Trace cells in lateral entorhinal cortex reflect the previous presence of a now missing object.
source: Interestingly, Tsao et al. (2013) recently reported 'trace cells' in lateral entorhinal cortex, whose firing reflects the previous presence of a now missing object, while related 'mis-place' cells have been reported in CA1 (O'Keefe, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tsao et al. (2013) and O'Keefe, 1976.

claim: Nominally non-spatially selective cells like perirhinal identity neurons can manifest a spatial trace firing field when re-activation occurs at the encoding location.
source: We have shown that nominally non-spatially selective cells like perirhinal identity neurons can manifest a spatial trace firing field when re-activation occurs at the encoding location (Figure 10D3).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 10D3.

claim: Humans can focus attention on different elements in an imagined scene, sampling one after another, without necessarily adopting a new imagined viewpoint.
source: Humans can focus attention on different elements in an imagined scene, sampling one after another, without necessarily adopting a new imagined viewpoint.
evidence: This is a well-known cognitive capability.

claim: Humans can localize an object in imagined scenes and retrieve its identity.
source: Moreover, humans can localize an object in imagined scenes and retrieve its identity (e.g. 'What was next to the fireplace in the restaurant we ate at?").
evidence: This is a well-known cognitive capability.

claim: Grid cell firing is thought to update the location represented by place cell firing, driven by signals relating to self-motion.
source: Grid cell (GC) firing is thought to update the location represented by place cell firing, driven by signals relating to self-motion (O'Keefe and Burgess, 2005; McNaughton et al., 2006; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Solstad et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Keefe and Burgess, 2005; McNaughton et al., 2006; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Solstad et al., 2006.

claim: Humans likely make use of spatial imagery even in apparently non-visual tasks such as triangle completion in darkness.
source: Indeed, humans likely make use of spatial imagery even in apparently non-visual tasks such as triangle completion in darkness (Tcheang et al., 2011), and there is evidence for grid-like brain activity during mental navigation (Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al. 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tcheang et al., 2011; Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al. 2016.

claim: Grid cells have been proposed to support the computation of vectors to a goal.
source: Grid cells have been proposed to support the computation of vectors to a goal (Kubie and Fenton, 2012; Erdem and Hasselmo, 2012; Bush et al., 2015; Stemmler et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kubie and Fenton, 2012; Erdem and Hasselmo, 2012; Bush et al., 2015; Stemmler et al., 2015.

claim: The model proposes that grid cells recruit new hippocampal cells (future place cells) in previously unexplored parts of a familiar environment.
source: We proposed that grid cells recruit new hippocampal cells (future place cells) in previously unexplored parts of a familiar environment (Figure 13 and Video 13).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim of the model, with reference to Figure 13 and Video 13.

claim: Planning a trajectory across unexplored space engenders preplay-like activity in place cells.
source: Planning a trajectory across unexplored space engenders preplay-like activity in place cells (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2015), whereas mental navigation is reminiscent of 'replay' (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011) or 'forward sweeps (Johnson and Redish, 2007; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2015), although the faster propagation speed (e.g. during sharp wave ripples) of these sequences of place cell activity are beyond the scope of the present model.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2015; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011; Johnson and Redish, 2007; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2015.

claim: It has been argued that the MTL-retrosplenial-parietal system supports the construction of coherent scenes.
source: It has been argued that the MTL-retrosplenial-parietal system supports the construction of coherent scenes (Burgess et al., 2001b; Byrne et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burgess et al., 2001b; Byrne et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010.

claim: If recollection corresponds to the reconstruction of something akin to a perceptual experience, then this places strong spatial constraints on how episodic memory works.
source: However, if recollection corresponds to the (re-)construction of something akin to a perceptual experience (the defining characteristic of episodic memory; Tulving 1985), then this places strong spatial constraints on how episodic memory works.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citation to Tulving 1985.

claim: Only a small subset of information combinations would be consistent with a single point of view, making episodic re-experiencing congruent with perceptual experiences.
source: A vast number of different combinations of information could be retrieved from the body of long-term knowledge in the MTL, but only a small subset would be consistent with a single point of view, making the episodic 're-experiencing' of events or visuo-spatial imagery congruent with perceptual experiences.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the constraints on episodic memory.

claim: The model distinguishes the egocentric representations supporting conscious re-experience from the more abstract allocentric representations involved in supporting computations.
source: This account includes functional roles for the specific firing characteristics of diverse populations of spatially selective cells across multiple brain regions, and distinguishes the egocentric representations supporting conscious (re-)experience from the more abstract (allocentric) representations involved in supporting computations.
evidence: This is a core theoretical claim of the model.

claim: The model follows Tulving's theoretical specification of episodic memory.
source: It follows Tulving's theoretical specification of episodic memory, and - spanning Marr's theoretical, algorithmic and implementational levels (Marr and Poggio, 1976) - bridges the gap between a neuropsychological description of spatial cognition (founded on behavioral and functional imaging data) and the neural representations supporting it.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marr and Poggio, 1976.

claim: The model spans Marr's theoretical, algorithmic and implementational levels.
source: It follows Tulving's theoretical specification of episodic memory, and - spanning Marr's theoretical, algorithmic and implementational levels (Marr and Poggio, 1976) - bridges the gap between a neuropsychological description of spatial cognition (founded on behavioral and functional imaging data) and the neural representations supporting it.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marr and Poggio, 1976.

claim: The model bridges the gap between a neuropsychological description of spatial cognition and the neural representations supporting it.
source: It follows Tulving's theoretical specification of episodic memory, and - spanning Marr's theoretical, algorithmic and implementational levels (Marr and Poggio, 1976) - bridges the gap between a neuropsychological description of spatial cognition (founded on behavioral and functional imaging data) and the neural representations supporting it.
evidence: This is a core claim about the contribution of the model.

claim: Object memory is superior when the target object is presented at the same position in the scene as it had been viewed originally.
source: Attaching representations of discrete objects (in the form of object vector cell activity) to a contextual representation via place cells aligns well with neuropsychological experiments that show position specificity in visual object memory (Hollingworth, 2007). In such experiments, object memory is superior when the target object is presented at the same position in the scene as it had been viewed originally (also see object novelty Simulations 1.3, 1.4).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hollingworth, 2007.

claim: The hippocampus in particular has been implicated in combining information about objects, locations, and contexts.
source: The hippocampus in particular has been implicated in combining information about objects, locations, and contexts (Warburton and Brown, 2010; Eacott and Gaffan, 2005; Barker and Warburton, 2015), consistent with the model.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Warburton and Brown, 2010; Eacott and Gaffan, 2005; Barker and Warburton, 2015.

claim: Studies suggest the hippocampus and precuneus are necessary for maintaining object-location binding even in working memory.
source: Similarly, studies suggest the hippocampus and precuneus are necessary for maintaining object-location binding even in working memory (Piekema et al., 2006; Olson et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Piekema et al., 2006; Olson et al., 2006.

claim: The direction-independence of place cell firing in open environments implies that all possible local views at a given location could be associated with the corresponding place cells.
source: The direction-independence of place cell firing in open environments implies that all possible local views at a given location could be associated with the corresponding place cells, potentially encompassing the boundaries in all directions around that location.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on known properties of place cells.

claim: Permanent landmarks should evoke stronger responses in retrosplenial cortex because they provide a more stable directional reference for the transformation circuit.
source: It also explains why permanent landmarks should evoke stronger responses in retrosplenial cortex (Auger et al., 2012), because permanent landmarks provide a more stable directional reference for the transformation circuit (see also Bicanski and Burgess, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Auger et al., 2012 and Bicanski and Burgess, 2016.

claim: Head direction cells likely serve to specify a direction of view, and not a movement direction.
source: In summary, head direction cells likely serve to specify a direction of view, and not a movement direction (Raudies et al., 2015), which could instead be expressed in the firing phase of grid cells or place cells (Maurer et al., 2014; Cei et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Raudies et al., 2015; Maurer et al., 2014; Cei et al., 2014.

claim: The encoding strategy for objects allows an agent to reactivate the set of place cells which were active when the object was encountered.
source: The encoding strategy for objects allows an agent to reactivate the set of place cells which were active when the object was encountered and thus reconstruct the local view at encoding in the parietal window.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about how the model supports recall.

claim: The model provides an explanation for the neural activity seen in the MTL, retrosplenial cortex and precuneus during imagery for familiar scenes.
source: This models the explicit recollection of a spatial scene populated with objects as an act of visuo-spatial imagery. It provides an explanation for the neural activity seen in the MTL, retrosplenial cortex and precuneus during imagery for familiar scenes (Burgess et al., 2001a; Hassabis et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burgess et al., 2001a; Hassabis et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007.

claim: The agent could use the place cells activated during imagery as 'goal cells' and use grid cells to calculate a vector to navigate to the remembered location.
source: The agent could also use the place cells activated during imagery as 'goal cells' and use grid cells to calculate a vector to navigate to the remembered location (Bush et al., 2015); not simulated here), accounting for the role of the MTL in goal-directed navigation (e.g. reviewed in Burgess et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bush et al., 2015 and Burgess et al., 2002.

claim: Not all memories for items requires reconstruction of a spatial scene.
source: However, not all memories for items requires reconstruction of a spatial scene.
evidence: This is a limitation of the model's scope.

claim: Recall of factual information (semantic memory) is not modeled.
source: Recall of factual information (semantic memory) is not modeled, while memory for the attributes of an object irrespective of its context would require only perirhinal involvement.
evidence: This is a limitation of the model's scope.

claim: The BB-model only applies to imagery for coherent spatial scenes.
source: The BB-model only applies to imagery for coherent spatial scenes, and suggests that this is necessary for episodic recollection in which the past event is 're-experienced' (Tulving, 1983), and certainly for remembering the spatial context of encountering an object.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tulving, 1983.

claim: By informing perception in a top-down manner, the MTL can effectively predict perceptual input in familiar environments.
source: By informing perception in a top-down manner, the MTL can effectively predict perceptual input in familiar environments, allowing novelty detection and enhancing perception with remembered information.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the function of top-down connections.

claim: If we view imagery as a top-down reconstruction of perceptual representations, the MTL together with the retrosplenial transformation circuit could be seen as a generative model for scenes.
source: If we view imagery as a top-down reconstruction of perceptual representations, the MTL together with the retrosplenial transformation circuit could be seen as a generative model for scenes, consistent with generative models of memory such as (Káli and Dayan, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Káli and Dayan, 2001.

claim: It has been proposed that the bottom-up/top-down transition between encoding and retrieving occurs rhythmically at the frequency of the theta rhythm.
source: It has been proposed that the bottom-up/top-down transition between encoding and retrieving occurs rhythmically at the frequency of the theta rhythm (Hasselmo et al., 1996; Burgess et al., 2001a; Hasselmo et al., 2002; Byrne et al., 2007; Douchamps et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hasselmo et al., 1996; Burgess et al., 2001a; Hasselmo et al., 2002; Byrne et al., 2007; Douchamps et al., 2013.

claim: Theta might underlie a periodic probing of memorized representations.
source: Theta might underlie a periodic probing of memorized representations; however, full recollection in imagery can last for long periods of time and need not correspond to specific phases of theta in humans (Düzel et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Düzel et al., 2010.

claim: The relative strength of top-down and bottom-up connections can change smoothly and under control of the agent to allow memory representations to influence neural activity during perception.
source: We have proposed (Figure 10) that the relative strength of top-down and bottom-up connections can change smoothly and under control of the agent (e.g. via the release of a neuromodulator) to allow memory representations to influence neural activity during perception.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim of the model, with reference to Figure 10.

claim: Tsao et al. (2013) recently reported 'trace cells' in lateral entorhinal cortex.
source: Interestingly, Tsao et al. (2013) recently reported 'trace cells' in lateral entorhinal cortex, whose firing reflects the previous presence of a now missing object, while related 'mis-place' cells have been reported in CA1 (O'Keefe, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tsao et al. (2013).

claim: The trace cells of Tsao et al. (2013) do not fire when the object is present, but only in the subsequent absence of the object.
source: However, the trace cells of Tsao et al. (2013) do not fire when the object is present, but only in the subsequent absence of the object. Thus they might signal the mismatch between the remembered object and its absence, that is reflecting a comparison of perceptually driven and memory driven firing of the model perirhinal cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings from Tsao et al. (2013).

claim: Attentional modulation in the present model is crucial for unambiguous representations of multiple objects within a scene.
source: Although we do not model the mechanistic origins of attention (see e.g. Itti and Koch, 2001), attentional modulation in the present model is crucial for unambiguous representations of multiple objects within a scene.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Itti and Koch, 2001.

claim: Objects must be sampled rhythmically and encoded sequentially in the parietal window.
source: Thus, we require the objects to be sampled rhythmically and encoded sequentially in the parietal window (Figures 3 and 11), consistent with experimental literature suggesting rhythmic and sequential sampling (VanRullen et al., 2007; Landau and Fries, 2012; for review see VanRullen, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to VanRullen et al., 2007; Landau and Fries, 2012; VanRullen, 2013, and reference to Figures 3 and 11.

claim: If attentional cycles have a limited duration, there may be insufficient time for activity to build up if there are too many objects within a scene, producing a capacity limit.
source: If attentional cycles have a limited duration, then there may be insufficient time for activity to build up in the corresponding neuronal populations and support robust encoding into memory if there are too many objects within a scene, producing a capacity limit (see also Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Bays and Husain, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Bays and Husain, 2008.

claim: The proposed binding of OVCs and PRo neurons, subject to attention, might provide a functional interpretation of the hippocampus' role in memory-guided attention.
source: The proposed binding of OVCs and PRo neurons, subject to attention, might also provide a functional interpretation of the hippocampus' role in memory-guided attention (e.g., Summerfield et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Summerfield et al., 2006.

claim: The model suggests a role for grid cell activity in human spatial cognition.
source: The model suggests a role for grid cell activity in human spatial cognition.
evidence: This is a core claim of the model.

claim: Humans likely make use of spatial imagery even in apparently non-visual tasks such as triangle completion in darkness.
source: Indeed, humans likely make use of spatial imagery even in apparently non-visual tasks such as triangle completion in darkness (Tcheang et al., 2011), and there is evidence for grid-like brain activity during mental navigation (Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al. 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tcheang et al., 2011; Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al. 2016.

claim: The model of mental navigation provides a mechanistic neural-level account of some aspects of 'scene construction' and 'episodic future thinking' with regard to familiar spaces.
source: The model of mental navigation provides a mechanistic neural-level account of some aspects of 'scene construction' and 'episodic future thinking' (Schacter et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010) with regard to familiar spaces.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schacter et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010.

claim: Mental navigation allows an agent to test future behavior, like the approach of a target from a new direction.
source: Mental navigation allows an agent to test future behavior, like the approach of a target from a new direction as depicted in Video 12.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Video 12.

claim: The same neural infrastructure involved in scene perception and reconstruction also subserves planning and hypothesis testing.
source: This suggests that the same neural infrastructure involved in scene perception and reconstruction also subserves planning and hypothesis testing (e.g. asking 'Which way should I go?' or 'What would I encounter if I went that way?').
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the function of the neural infrastructure.

claim: The model suggests that sweeps of activity in the grid cell population may play a role in replay, forward sweeps, and could correspond to route planning.
source: Nevertheless, the model suggests that sweeps of activity in the grid cell population may play are role in these aspects of place cell firing, and could correspond to route planning (Kubie and Fenton, 2012; Erdem and Hasselmo, 2012; Bush et al., 2015; Yamamoto and Tonegawa, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kubie and Fenton, 2012; Erdem and Hasselmo, 2012; Bush et al., 2015; Yamamoto and Tonegawa, 2017.
